lumen-capital.desc: A reserved identity and editorial site for a thesis-driven investment firm.
lumen-capital.problem: Lumen had spent two years quietly compounding returns on a thesis few funds were running. Their website was a placeholder put up the day they incorporated. Every introduction from a friend ended with the same line: "Don’t look at the site." It was the first thing every founder they wanted to back saw.
approach: We started with a week of reading — every memo Lumen had written, every Q′ly letter to LPs, the books on Mira’s shelf. The voice was already there; the site just needed to honour it.
Identity is a quiet sans wordmark and a single editorial mark — the ‘L’ set to do the work of a logo and a footer ornament both. Type is Tiempos Headline paired with Söhne. No icons. No diagrams.
The site is one long scroll: thesis, portfolio, team, contact. Type carries the argument. Numbers are deliberately understated — what looks like restraint reads as confidence.
spreads: Wordmark studies — 47 directions narrowed to 3
Homepage hero, in-situ, on a 13″ MacBook
Thesis spread — type-driven argument, no illustrations
Portfolio company grid — every logo at the same x-height
Mobile case-study reader — single column
LP report template — Figma file shipped alongside

quote.text: We weren’t looking for a ‘designer.’ We were looking for someone to make us look like ourselves. David did that in fourteen weeks and made me feel embarrassed I hadn’t commissioned it sooner.

lumen-capital.rework: I’d push back harder on the team-bio length. We ended up with paragraphs longer than the thesis page itself — vanity sneaking in at the last mile.
lumen-capital.seoDescription: Brand identity and editorial website for Lumen Capital — a thesis-driven investment firm. Reserved typographic system, custom CMS, single voice.
lumen-capital.ogImageAlt: Lumen Capital — Brand & Website by David Almoalem

tessera-studio.desc: Visual system and site for an architectural practice in Athens.
tessera-studio.problem: Tessera had been working out of Athens for nine years with a Wordpress site they couldn’t change without calling their nephew. A 2025 win at the Mies prize meant the inbound went vertical — and the site stayed in 2017.
approach: Three weeks in Athens. We worked from the studio, sat in their pin-ups, photographed every project they’d ever shipped on a Mamiya 7.
The site is built around the photography — monochrome plates that take up the full screen, captions in a 11pt mono, never on the image.
No ‘Projects’ tab. The work IS the navigation. You scroll vertically and you’re in the next project. Each one carries its year as the only chrome.
spreads: Identity — a single wordmark, two weights
Photography direction — black-and-white, single-source light
Homepage as project gallery, vertically scrolled
Project detail — captions never overlay images
Practice page — a single paragraph, hand-typeset

quote.text: He folded into our practice for six months and made everything around him quieter and more confident. The work is genuinely beautiful — and our nephew can still edit it.

tessera-studio.rework: The Greek typography on the about-page wants more love. Greek small-caps are their own problem and we shipped without fully solving it.
tessera-studio.seoDescription: Visual system and Webflow site for Tessera Studio — an architectural practice in Athens. Quiet wordmark, modular grid, slow editorial rhythm.
tessera-studio.ogImageAlt: Tessera Studio — Identity & Webflow by David Almoalem

halcyon-museum.desc: A scrollable exhibition for the museum's spring archive opening.
halcyon-museum.problem: Halcyon wanted to put a 12-month exhibition online. Not as a marketing site — as a serious scrollable exhibition that could outlive the in-person show.
approach: Curatorial collaboration from week one. The chief curator and I co-edited the scroll like a magazine spread.
Each room of the exhibition is a section. Within each section, you scroll laterally through the works. Captions, provenance, conservation notes all hang together at the same y-position.
Built with WebGL for the cover gestures — a slow pan over a high-res scan, parallax depth from a single image. Falls back gracefully on lower devices.
spreads: Cover — WebGL parallax over a 1.2 GB scan
Room I — horizontal scroll, vertical captions
Conservation notes — inline footnote system
Audio guide — transcripts as scrollable annotations
About the curator — a single-column letter

quote.text: Working with David made the exhibition feel like a print magazine that happened to live in a browser. That sounds simple. It is not.

halcyon-museum.rework: Audio guide controls should have been simpler. We over-engineered a transport that 80% of visitors never used.
halcyon-museum.seoDescription: A scrollable React exhibition for Halcyon Museum's spring archive opening. Considered motion, archival type, accessible across reading levels.
halcyon-museum.ogImageAlt: Halcyon Museum — Exhibition site by David Almoalem

object-and-form.desc: Editorial commerce for a small-batch homeware brand.
object-and-form.problem: Yael had built Object & Form on Instagram — small batches, sold out within the hour. She wanted a real shop without losing the ‘email a friend a photograph’ feel.
approach: Shopify, used unapologetically as a CMS — not a store. The cart lives in a small drawer; the rest of the site is editorial.
Every product has a long-form essay attached: the maker, the kiln, the misfires, the names. You buy a story.
Restock notifications by SMS — short, like Yael writing to you herself.
spreads: Wordmark — a wide serif, one weight
Product page — essay above the buy button
Drop page — single hero, restock SMS embedded
Maker bios — photographed at the kiln

quote.text: I’ve worked with three studios in Tel Aviv. David is the only one who gave me the unglamorous answers I needed — and then designed something better than the glamorous ones promised.

object-and-form.rework: Wishlist was a feature creep we both regretted. Should have shipped without it; sales would not have been worse.
object-and-form.seoDescription: Editorial commerce on Shopify for Object & Form — a small-batch homeware brand. Wordmark, lookbook system, product storytelling that converts.
object-and-form.ogImageAlt: Object & Form — E-commerce by David Almoalem

northbound.desc: Repositioning and website for a logistics platform raising Series B.
northbound.problem: Northbound was raising Series B with a 2018 site they’d outgrown four times over. Their pitch deck was beautiful. Their site looked like the company they used to be.
approach: Repositioning first, design second. Three days of interviews with sales reps and customer success — the friction was in the language, not the layout.
Built a long marketing site with a clear hierarchy: who, what for whom, how it works, why now, what it costs.
Each ‘how it works’ step is a scroll-locked diagram — plain SVG, no Lottie, no video.
spreads: Wordmark refresh — same monogram, new wordmark
Homepage — the new positioning, in two sentences
How-it-works — 4 scroll-locked SVG diagrams
Pricing page — honest, three tiers, no ‘contact us’
Customer stories — short, with named numbers

quote.text: We raised in the room the deck had set up — but the site is what kept the call going past the first awkward minute.

northbound.rework: I should have insisted on photography. The illustrative placeholders we used became permanent and the site lost an opportunity to feel human.
northbound.seoDescription: Repositioning and marketing site for Northbound — a logistics platform raising Series B. Diagrams that explain, pricing that doesn't hide.
northbound.ogImageAlt: Northbound — SaaS site by David Almoalem

atelier-cote.desc: From wordmark to wayfinding for a coastal hospitality group.
atelier-cote.problem: Atelier Côte was opening their second property on a stretch of coast nobody had heard of. They needed a brand that could carry from a hand-painted lobby sign to a 13′′ booking confirmation email.
approach: Started with the sign painter. The wordmark was hand-lettered first, then digitised, never the other way around.
Print first — menus, key-cards, way-finding, the bottle for the in-room oil. The site was the last thing we made and it shows.
Site is a single page — photography of the property, two paragraphs, a booking widget. Nothing else.
spreads: Wordmark — hand-painted, then digitised
Way-finding — signage at the property
Stationery — letterhead, key-card, oil bottle
Site — single page, four photographs
Email — confirmation, with the wordmark

quote.text: We sold out the first season before the second wave of press even ran. David made an identity that earned us trust before guests had set foot on the path.

atelier-cote.rework: We left the website too thin. A second ‘Stay’ page would have caught the long-form-readers we kept losing to the inbox.
atelier-cote.seoDescription: Hand-lettered wordmark to web for Atelier Côte — a coastal hospitality group. Sign painting, stationery, single-page booking site that prints.
atelier-cote.ogImageAlt: Atelier Côte — Brand & Print by David Almoalem
